selvfølgelig.explanation: "Selvfølgelig" means "of course". To agree to a request right away, answer with it: "Kan du hjælpe mig?" "Selvfølgelig!" (Can you help me? Of course!) To say something happened as expected, put it inside the sentence: "Hun kommer selvfølgelig for sent" (Of course she is going to be late).

selvglad.explanation: "Selvglad" means "smug". It is built from "selv" (self) and "glad" (happy), so it is literally "happy with oneself". To say you are pleased with your own work in a good way, use "tilfreds" (satisfied): "Jeg er tilfreds med min indsats" (I am satisfied with my effort).

selvmodsigende.explanation: "Selvmodsigende" means "contradictory". It is built from "selv" (self) and "at modsige" (to contradict), so it contradicts itself. To say that an explanation does not agree with itself: "Hans forklaring er selvmodsigende" (His explanation is contradictory).

selvom.explanation: "Selvom" means "even though". To say something happens in spite of a fact, put it before the fact: "Jeg går en tur, selvom det regner" (I am going for a walk even though it is raining). To give just the noun instead of a whole clause, use "på trods af" (despite): "Jeg går en tur på trods af regnen" (I am going for a walk despite the rain).

selvsikker.explanation: "Selvsikker" means "confident". It is built from "selv" (self) and "sikker" (sure). "Selv" also begins other words, such as "selvstændig" (independent).

selvstændig.explanation: "Selvstændig" means "independent". When you say a grown person runs their own business, it means "self-employed": "Min søster er selvstændig" (My sister is self-employed).

selvstændighed.explanation: "Selvstændighed" means "independence". It is built from "selvstændig" (independent) and the ending "-hed", which makes a noun. To say a person learns to manage alone: "Børn lærer selvstændighed" (Children learn independence). To say a country wants to be free: "Landet kæmper for sin selvstændighed" (The country is fighting for its independence).

selvtillid.explanation: "Selvtillid" means "self-confidence". It is built from "selv" (self) and "tillid" (trust). To say someone is missing self-confidence: "Han mangler selvtillid" (He lacks self-confidence).

senere.explanation: "Senere" means "later". To say later on the same day: "senere i dag" (later today). Do not mix it up with "sent" (late in time): "Det er sent" (It is late).

seneste.explanation: "Seneste" means "latest". To talk about the newest thing someone made: "Har du set hans seneste film?" (Have you seen his latest movie?) To talk about the recent past: "de seneste uger" (the last few weeks). To talk about the final one in a row, use "sidste" (last): "Det er den sidste bus" (It is the last bus).

sengetid.explanation: "Sengetid" means "bedtime". It is built from "seng" (bed) and "tid" (time). "Tid" also ends other words for set times, such as "spisetid" (mealtime).

sennep.explanation: "Sennep" means "mustard". When you talk about mustard in general, leave out "en": "Vil du have sennep på?" (Do you want mustard on it?) To say a small amount, use "en klat sennep" (a dollop of mustard).

sensitiv.explanation: "Sensitiv" means "sensitive", for skin, teeth or a child who reacts easily. "Følsom" also means "sensitive" and is used for feelings: "Han er meget følsom" (He is very sensitive).

sent.explanation: "Sent" means "late". To say you arrived after the expected time: "Vi kom sent" (We came late). Do not mix it up with "senere" (later): "Vi kommer senere" (We will come later). To say you are too late, use "for sent": "Jeg kommer for sent" (I am coming too late).

september.explanation: "September" means "September". In Danish, month names are not capitalized. To say something happens in that month: "Vi rejser i september" (We travel in September).

seriøs.explanation: "Seriøs" means "serious". To ask whether someone is not joking: "Er du seriøs?" (Are you serious?)

ses i morgen.explanation: "Ses i morgen" means "see you tomorrow". "Ses" is short for "vi ses" (we see each other). To say you will meet that evening instead, change the time: "Ses i aften" (See you tonight).

sexet.explanation: "Sexet" means "sexy". English speakers should note that it ends in "-et", not "-y". To describe a car: "Bilen er sexet" (The car is sexy).

shampoo.explanation: "Shampoo" means "shampoo" and is spelled the same as in English. It takes "en" ("shampooen" is the form with "the"), but when you talk about some shampoo, leave out "en": "Har du noget shampoo?" (Do you have any shampoo?) To count it by the bottle: "en flaske shampoo" (a bottle of shampoo).

shorts.explanation: "Shorts" means "shorts". Danish treats it as plural, as English does. To talk about one pair, say "et par shorts" (a pair of shorts): "Mine shorts er nye" (My shorts are new).

siddende.explanation: "Siddende" means "seated". It comes from the verb "at sidde" (to sit). When you talk about whoever holds an office right now, it means "sitting": "den siddende regering" (the sitting government).

siden.explanation: "Siden" means "since". To say when something began, name the time after it: "siden i går" (since yesterday). It also means "ago". To say how long before now, put it last: "for to år siden" (two years ago).

sidenhen.explanation: "Sidenhen" means "since then". It is built from "siden" (since). To say how things changed after a moment in the past: "Han var genert som barn, men sidenhen er han blevet mere åben" (He was shy as a child, but since then he has become more open).

sidst.explanation: "Sidst" means "last". To say "the last time", use "sidste" before the noun: "Det var sidste gang" (That was the last time).

sidste.explanation: "Sidste" means "last". To point to the final one before a noun: "den sidste bus" (the last bus). To name a recent period of time: "sidste uge" (last week). To say you came after everyone else, use "sidst": "Jeg kom sidst" (I came last).

sig.explanation: "Sig" means "himself". It also means "herself", "itself" and "themselves". When the person doing the action and the person receiving it are the same, use "sig": "Han vasker sig" (He washes himself). When they are two different people, use "ham" (him): "Han vasker ham" (He washes him). Some verbs always go with "sig". To say you look forward to something, use "at glæde sig": "Børnene glæder sig til jul" (The children look forward to Christmas).

sikke.explanation: "Sikke" means "what a" and starts an exclamation. With a word that takes "en", say: "Sikke en overraskelse!" (What a surprise!) With a word that takes "et", say: "Sikke et vejr!" (What weather!)

sikke en dag.explanation: "Sikke en dag" means "what a day". To react to a day that was hard, say: "Sikke en dag! Jeg er helt udmattet." (What a day! I am completely worn out.) "Sikke en" goes before a word that takes "en". Before a word that takes "et", use "sikke et": "Sikke et vejr!" (What weather!)

sikke noget.explanation: "Sikke noget" means "wow". To react to something that surprised you, add the thing you noticed: "Sikke noget vejr!" (What weather!)

sikker.explanation: "Sikker" means "safe". To say something cannot hurt you: "Cyklen er sikker" (The bike is safe). When you have no doubt, it means "sure": "Er du sikker?" (Are you sure?)

sikkerhed.explanation: "Sikkerhed" means "security", as in being protected from harm. It is built from "sikker" (safe) and the ending "-hed", which makes a noun. To say you know something for sure, use "med sikkerhed": "Jeg ved det med sikkerhed" (I know it for sure).

sild.explanation: "Sild" means "herring". The plural is the same word. To name herring in a marinade, say: "marineret sild" (pickled herring).

silke.explanation: "Silke" means "silk". When you talk about the material, use it without an article: "Jeg elsker silke" (I love silk). When it starts a longer word, it names what something is made of: "et silketørklæde" (a silk scarf).

simpel.explanation: "Simpel" means "simple". To describe a house with nothing extra: "Det er et simpelt hus" (It is a plain house).

simpelthen.explanation: "Simpelthen" means "simply". To add force to a statement, put it before the word it strengthens: "Jeg kan simpelthen ikke lide det" (I simply do not like it).

sin.explanation: "Sin" means "his own". It also means "her own" and "its own". It goes before a word that takes "en" and points back to the person doing the action: "Peter ser sin bror" (Peter sees his own brother). When the brother belongs to someone else, use "hans" (his): "Peter ser Jens og hans bror" (Peter sees Jens and Jens's brother). For "I" and "you", use "min" (my) and "din" (your): "Jeg ser min bror" (I see my brother).

sindssyg.explanation: "Sindssyg" means "insane". It is built from "sind" (mind) and "syg" (sick). To say something is extremely good: "Det er sindssygt godt" (It is insanely good).

sine.explanation: "Sine" means "his own". It also means "her own". It goes before more than one thing: "Peter ser sine venner" (Peter sees his own friends). When the friends belong to someone else, use "hans" (his): "Peter ser Jens og hans venner" (Peter sees Jens and Jens's friends). For one thing that takes "en", use "sin": "sin bror" (his own brother). For one thing that takes "et", use "sit": "sit hus" (his own house).

single.explanation: "Single" means "single", as in not being in a relationship. It is spelled the same as in English. To say "just one" of something, use "enkelt": "en enkelt dag" (a single day).

sirup.explanation: "En sirup" means "a syrup". Do not mix it up with "saft" (fruit cordial, which you mix with water): "Vil du have saft?" (Do you want some cordial?)

sit.explanation: "Sit" means "his own". It also means "her own" and "its own". It goes before a word that takes "et" and points back to the person doing the action: "Peter elsker sit hus" (Peter loves his own house). When the house belongs to someone else, use "hans" (his): "Peter ser Jens og hans hus" (Peter sees Jens and Jens's house). Before a word that takes "en", use "sin": "sin bil" (his own car).

sjette.explanation: "Sjette" means "sixth". English speakers might expect it to look like "seks" (six), but it is spelled "sjette", not "sekste". To give a date: "den sjette maj" (the sixth of May).

sjov.explanation: "Sjov" means "fun". To say you enjoyed something: "Det var sjovt" (That was fun). It also means "funny", for something that makes you laugh: "en sjov vittighed" (a funny joke). To say you did something as a joke: "Jeg gjorde det for sjov" (I did it as a joke).

sjusket.explanation: "Sjusket" means "sloppy". To describe work done too fast: "Han lavede et sjusket stykke arbejde" (He did a sloppy job).

sjælden.explanation: "Sjælden" means "rare". To say a thing is hard to find: "Den bog er sjælden" (That book is rare). Do not mix it up with "sjældent" (rarely), which describes how seldom you do something: "Jeg ser ham sjældent" (I rarely see him).

sjældent.explanation: "Sjældent" means "rarely". To say you do something seldom: "Han kommer sjældent for sent" (He is rarely late). For something hard to find, use "sjælden": "Den bog er sjælden" (That book is rare).

skadelig.explanation: "Skadelig" means "harmful". It is built from "skade" (harm) and the ending "-lig". To say something damages your health: "skadelig for helbredet" (harmful to health).

skak.explanation: "Skak" means "chess". It has no article when you talk about the game: "Han er god til skak" (He is good at chess). In the game, shout "Skak!" (Check!) when the king is under attack. The game ends with "skak mat" (checkmate).

skal vi ikke bare...?.explanation: "Skal vi ikke bare...?" means "shall we just...?". It is literally "shall we not just...?". To suggest the easy option: "Det regner. Skal vi ikke bare tage hjem?" (It is raining. Shall we just go home?)

skaldet.explanation: "Skaldet" means "bald". To say a man is starting to lose his hair, use "ved at blive" (in the middle of becoming): "Han er ved at blive skaldet" (He is going bald).

skaldyr.explanation: "Skaldyr" means "shellfish". It is built from "skal" (shell) and "dyr" (animal). To say you cannot eat shellfish because of an allergy: "Jeg er allergisk over for skaldyr" (I am allergic to shellfish). It has no article when you talk about shellfish in general.

skam.explanation: "Skam" means "shame". To say asking is nothing to be ashamed of: "Der er ingen skam i at spørge" (There is no shame in asking). It also means "a pity" in "en skam": "Det er en skam, at du ikke kan komme" (It is a pity that you cannot come).

skamfuld.explanation: "Skamfuld" means "ashamed". It is built from "skam" (shame) and "fuld" (full), so it is literally "full of shame". To say what you are ashamed of, add "over" (about): "Jeg er skamfuld over, hvad jeg gjorde" (I am ashamed of what I did).

skandinavien.explanation: "Skandinavien" means "Scandinavia". Place names such as "Skandinavien" start with a big first letter in Danish, but "skandinavisk" (Scandinavian) does not. To include Finland and Iceland too, say "Norden" (the Nordic countries): "Island hører til Norden" (Iceland belongs to the Nordic countries).

skarp.explanation: "Skarp" means "sharp". To say a blade cuts well: "Kniven er skarp" (The knife is sharp). To say someone thinks quickly: "Hun er meget skarp" (She is very sharp).

skarpt.explanation: "Skarpt" means "sharply". To describe a cutting tone of voice: "Han svarede skarpt" (He answered sharply). To describe a sudden, steep turn: "Vejen drejer skarpt til højre" (The road turns sharply to the right). To say a thing itself is sharp, use "skarp": "Kniven er skarp" (The knife is sharp).

skeptisk.explanation: "Skeptisk" means "skeptical". To say which idea you doubt, add "over for" (about): "Jeg er skeptisk over for planen" (I am skeptical about the plan).

skidt.explanation: "Skidt" means "bad". To say something went better than expected: "Det gik ikke så skidt" (It did not go so badly). To say you do not care about a problem, say "Skidt med det" (Never mind). It also means "dirt": "Der er skidt på dine sko" (There is dirt on your shoes).

skiløb.explanation: "Skiløb" means "skiing". It is built from "ski" (ski) and "løb" (run). To say you ski, use "at stå på ski" (literally, to stand on skis): "Jeg står på ski hver vinter" (I ski every winter). It also means "a ski race": "Han vandt skiløbet" (He won the ski race).

skinnende.explanation: "Skinnende" means "shiny". It comes from the verb "at skinne" (to shine). To describe jewelry that catches the light: "en skinnende ring" (a shiny ring).

sko.explanation: "Sko" means "shoes". When you talk about more than one shoe, the word does not change: "to sko" (two shoes). To say you put your shoes on, Danish says "the shoes" where English says "my shoes": "Jeg tager skoene på" (I put my shoes on).

skrald.explanation: "Skrald" means "garbage". It takes "et" (the form with "the" is "skraldet"). To say you carry the garbage outside: "Jeg tager skraldet ud" (I take the garbage out). The container is "en skraldespand" (a garbage can).

skriftlig.explanation: "Skriftlig" means "written". To name the opposite, for things done by speaking, use "mundtlig" (oral): "en mundtlig prøve" (an oral test).

skråt.explanation: "Skråt" means "at an angle". To say where something is diagonally across from something else, use "skråt over for": "Caféen ligger skråt over for stationen" (The cafe is diagonally across from the station).

skræk.explanation: "Skræk" means "fright". To say someone screamed because of sudden fear: "Hun skreg af skræk" (She screamed in terror). Do not mix it up with "en bekymring" (a worry), which lasts: "Jeg har en bekymring for pengene" (I have a worry about money).

skræmmende.explanation: "Skræmmende" means "frightening". To say how you feel, use "bange" (scared): "Jeg er bange" (I am scared).

skræmt.explanation: "Skræmt" means "scared". It comes from the verb "at skræmme" (to scare). To name what you are afraid of, use "bange for": "Jeg er bange for edderkopper" (I am afraid of spiders).

skrøbelig.explanation: "Skrøbelig" means "frail". It describes a weak, old or sick person. When you say something breaks easily, it means "fragile": "Glasset er skrøbeligt" (The glass is fragile). To describe something that could easily collapse, such as a peace: "en skrøbelig fred" (a fragile peace).

skuffende.explanation: "Skuffende" means "disappointing". To say a person feels let down, use "skuffet" (disappointed): "Jeg er skuffet" (I am disappointed).

skuffet.explanation: "Skuffet" means "disappointed". It describes how a person feels. For what let you down, use "skuffende" (disappointing): "Filmen var skuffende" (The film was disappointing).

skummetmælk.explanation: "Skummetmælk" means "skim milk". It is built from "skummet" (skimmed) and "mælk" (milk). To ask for a drink: "Jeg vil gerne have et glas skummetmælk" (I would like a glass of skim milk).

sky.explanation: "Sky" means "shy". Do not mix it up with "en sky" (a cloud), which is spelled the same: "Hun er sky" (She is shy), but "Der er en sky på himlen" (There is a cloud in the sky).

skyet.explanation: "Skyet" means "cloudy". It comes from "en sky" (a cloud). When clouds cover the whole sky, use "overskyet" (overcast): "Det er overskyet i dag" (It is overcast today).

skyld.explanation: "Skyld" means "guilt". When you say who caused a problem, it means "fault": "Det er ikke din skyld" (It is not your fault). To ask who is to blame: "Hvem har skylden?" (Who is to blame?)

skyldfølelse.explanation: "En skyldfølelse" means "a feeling of guilt". It is built from "skyld" (guilt) and "følelse" (feeling). To say you feel bad about something, say: "Jeg har dårlig samvittighed" (I feel bad about it). It is literally "I have a bad conscience".

skyldig.explanation: "Skyldig" means "guilty". When you say you owe someone money, it means "owing": "Jeg er dig 50 kroner skyldig" (I owe you 50 kroner).

skynd dig.explanation: "Skynd dig" means "hurry up". The small word "dig" means "yourself", so you say it to one person. To tell several people to hurry, use "jer" (yourselves) instead: "Skynd jer, bussen kommer!" (Hurry up, the bus is coming!)

skyr.explanation: "Skyr" means "skyr". It is a dairy food that came to Denmark from Iceland. When you talk about skyr in general, use no article: "Jeg spiser skyr til morgenmad" (I eat skyr for breakfast).

skål.explanation: "Skål" means "cheers". To toast a person, add "for" and the name: "Skål for Anna!" (Cheers to Anna!) The same word also means "a bowl": "en skål med frugt" (a bowl of fruit).

skærtorsdag.explanation: "Skærtorsdag" means "Maundy Thursday". It is the Thursday before "langfredag" (Good Friday). It is a public holiday in Denmark.

skæv.explanation: "Skæv" means "crooked". To describe a line or a picture that is not straight: "Billedet hænger skævt" (The picture hangs crooked). For a humor that is odd, it means "quirky": "en skæv humor" (a quirky sense of humor).

skødesløs.explanation: "Skødesløs" means "careless". To say someone does not look after their belongings: "Han er skødesløs med sine ting" (He is careless with his things).

skøjteløb.explanation: "Skøjteløb" means "ice skating". It is built from "skøjte" (ice skate) and "løb" (run). To say you go ice skating, use "at løbe på skøjter" (literally, to run on skates): "Vi løber på skøjter i weekenden" (We go ice skating at the weekend).

skønt.explanation: "Skønt" means "although" and joins two parts of a sentence: "Jeg gik, skønt det regnede" (I went although it rained). To say the same with "selvom" (even though): "Jeg gik, selvom det regnede" (I went even though it rained). The same spelling also means "lovely": "Det er skønt!" (That is lovely!)

skør.explanation: "Skør" means "crazy". To tell a friend they are being silly: "Du er skør!" (You are crazy!)

sladder.explanation: "Sladder" means "gossip". It takes "en" (the form with "the" is "sladderen"). To say people talk a lot about others: "Der er meget sladder på kontoret" (There is a lot of gossip at the office). A person who spreads it is "en sladrehank" (a tattletale): "Han er en sladrehank" (He is a tattletale).

sladrevorn.explanation: "Sladrevorn" means "gossipy". It comes from the verb "at sladre" (to gossip). To describe a small place where everyone talks about each other: "en sladrevorn by" (a gossipy town).

slank.explanation: "Slank" means "slim". It is used for things too: "en slank mobil" (a slim phone).

slet ikke.explanation: "Slet ikke" means "not at all". To make a no stronger: "Jeg er slet ikke træt" (I am not at all tired). Without "slet", it is a plain no: "Jeg er ikke træt" (I am not tired).

slidt.explanation: "Slidt" means "worn". To say you are completely exhausted: "Jeg er helt slidt" (I am completely worn out).

slik.explanation: "Slik" means "candy". It takes "et" (the form with "the" is "slikket"), but when you mean candy in general, leave out the article: "Jeg spiser for meget slik" (I eat too much candy). Danes have a word for candy eaten on Saturdays: "lørdagsslik" (literally, Saturday candy).

slud.explanation: "Slud" means "sleet". Do not mix it up with "hagl" (hail): "Der falder hagl" (Hail is falling).

slut.explanation: "Slut" means "over". To say an event has ended, use it after "er" (is): "Filmen er slut" (The movie is over). When you say supplies are gone, it means "all gone": "Mælken er slut" (The milk has run out).

sløret.explanation: "Sløret" means "blurred". To say something is hinted at on purpose, use "tilsløret" (veiled): "en tilsløret trussel" (a veiled threat).

smagløs.explanation: "Smagløs" means "tasteless". It is built from "smag" (taste) and "-løs" (without). For food with no flavor: "Suppen er smagløs" (The soup is tasteless). For a remark in bad taste: "Det var en smagløs bemærkning" (That was a tasteless remark).

smal.explanation: "Smal" means "narrow". Do not mix it up with "tynd" (thin), which describes thickness: "et tyndt papir" (a thin sheet of paper).

smart.explanation: "Smart" means "clever". For clothes that look stylish, it means "stylish": "en smart jakke" (a stylish jacket). For a person who is intelligent, use "klog" (smart): "Hun er klog" (She is smart).

smertefuld.explanation: "Smertefuld" means "painful". It is built from "smerte" (pain) and "fuld" (full). To say a body part hurts right now, use "at gøre ondt" (to hurt): "Det gør ondt" (It hurts).

smertelig.explanation: "Smertelig" means "painful". Do not mix it up with "smertefuld" (painful), which is a different word: "en smertefuld skade" (a painful injury).

smertestillende.explanation: "Smertestillende" means "painkillers". It is short for "smertestillende midler" (pain-relieving medicines). To ask a pharmacist: "Har I noget smertestillende?" (Do you have any painkillers?)
